Press Release:


Boiling Point
Gun shots echo through the informal settlement in Kya Sands as hundreds of rock-throwing protesters clash with armed police. It seems like just an ordinary day in South Africa, and just another service delivery protest over empty political promises. But, in the heart of many impoverished communities, tempers are flaring and angry protesters know that only through violence will their message be heard. From Port Elizabeth to Johannesburg, Carte Blanche takes to the streets to ask whether government has lost touch with its people.


Script:


Script – Boiling point

VO: 27
Promises were made at the ANC National General Council last weekend. But by early Monday morning a violent service delivery protest broke out north of Johannesburg. Angry residents of Kyasands and Msawawa informal settlements disrupted peak hour traffic by blocking arterial routes. Police resorted to firing rubber bullets in an attempt to control the crowds.
(nat sound)

They were protesting for houses. A NUMSA member representing the community addressed the crowds.

Community leader:
The fact is we cannot be moved from an informal settlement to another informal settlement.

VO: 7”
Once a measure of order returned the protesters demanded to see the MEC of Human Settlements to hand over a memorandum.

Upsound:
Amandla! Amandla!

VO: 8
The MEC sent a representative a Director in his department to listen to their demands for housing and proper services. But visit Kyasands informal settlement and it doesn’t take long to realize why these people have taken their frustration to the streets.

Link

For the people who live here in Kya Sands informal settlement where there is no no water, no sanitation, no electricity and the rubbish is literally piling up in the streets, the only thing on offer here is empty promises.

VO: 10
These tattered blue documents are what Ma Miriam holds onto as the promise of her house. She’ll be sixty this year and 15 years ago she was given this piece of paper.

Claire:
Where was it going to be?

Miriam:
They promised the house would be at Cosmo City.


VO: 23
Cosmo city is a flagship housing development just up the road. But as the years wore on their hopes diminished. Now they’ve been told that the old lion park premises nearby will be developed into a low cost housing for them but the housing dept says they are battling to find funding for the necessary infrastructure.

Housing: Director: Vulindlela Mapekhulu
The major stumbling block at the moment is that we need to install a bulk sewer here. The Department is in discussions with the Department of water affairs to avail the more than one billion rand that is required.

VO: 11”
For residents patience is running thin. Miriam lives in these cramped quarters with her husband and 6 grandchildren, most of whom sleep on the floor.

Miriam:
I put a sponge on the floor so that they can sleep here. It becomes hard for them because they have to wake up early in the morning for school because they are sleeping in the kitchen.

VO: 12”
People on the ground are increasingly feeling like they don’t have a voice says Professor Tinyiko Maluleke so it’s little wonder they resort to protesting.

Prof:
This is the way SA’s have spoken to their rulers for a long time. I think the language needs to improve and the arguments need to improve on both sides. The communication needs to be improved.

VO:
Street blockades are one of the weapons of the week to get attention says Patrick Bond from the School for Governance at Wits.

Patrick:
We’re finding new tactics that suggest that they are thinking about power in creative ways – one of them is the obvious street blockades, so it shows if you want to shut a place down, go for the arterial routes, the spokes within a very vulnerable transport system.

VO: 7”
Vast inequalities between rich and poor living side by side is a powder keg for a land war.

Prof:
That situation is volatile but in a slow cooker way. The poor are adding more and more shacks to the side of town and the big developers are setting up all sorts of magnificent developments there. They are very expensive places and I don’t know what’s going to happen.

VO:
Which is why tempers reached boiling point in Kyasands.

Claire link @ police car
Violent service delivery protests like this one are an almot daily occurrence – they reflect a growing and simmering dissent.

VO: 32
It’s a theme that plays out over and over again. Last year it was reported that we had staggering 1907 violent service delivery protests – the kind of figures you’re likely to see in a country experiencing civil war. Across the country in the Nelson Mandela Metro these protests spilt over on the streets twice in recent months. The first time in July around the issue of education in the poverty stricken northern suburbs. There were running gun battles in the streets between police and children. Northern Areas Education forum leader Richard Draai says it was a last resort.

Richard: (41)
We exhausted all avenues to address the quality education of our children….the last resort was to usse our children at the forefront of the protest action.

VO: 15
All they wanted was a paid teacher in every class and support staff to ensure their children had a chance at a future. Schools were shut down and learners vented their anger at the task force who tried to keep the situation under control. It was chaos.

Richard: (46)
The protests is something I want to rub out of my life forever.

VO: 11”
Vandalism was rife and cars were stoned in the opportunistic violence that followed. The ANC dispatched the education MEC in an attempt to quell the situation.
There’s been some relief but many of the promises made were not met.

Richard: (46)
Currently there’s over 120 vacancies and 30 teachers, educators still must be paid. We have one in our school and I cry with her every time I speak to her.

VO: 16
Then in August the streets of Walmer an upmarket Port Elizabeth suburb erupted when protestors from the Walmer township took to the streets to demonstrate their frustration with lack of housing and services. Richard Dubana took part in that strike.

Richard Dubana: (25)
We are voting for the wrong people. We are choosing the wrong people to be our council, our committee, then they don’t do the job.

VO: 10
The protesters ransacked the swish Walmer country club leaving a trail of destruction behind them. The root cause of these protests is often money.

Patrick:
They do run out of money, they are not just wasting money. They are not just throwing money back that they can’t spend and if they are throwing money back that they can’t spend, its because of policy.

VO: 11”
Against the backdrop of dire socio economic conditions with around 54% of South Africans living on R750 a day he believes the anger is justified.

Patrick:
You ask why so many, why such anger? The socio economic conditions are unbearable. 54% poverty, unemployment that probably should be measured at 40% if you include everybody not working.

VO: 14”
The ANC admits that the previous leadership in the metro has failed the people, which is why they appointed Danny Jordaan as part of their rescue plan. They’re concerned that they could lose the PE metro says spokesman Zizi Kodwa.

Zizi:
The ANC as an organization could have good leaders, but the reflection of that good leadership is in the municipality. Remember that the national cabinet has now appoved 4.6 billion that will be deployed in the Nelson Mandela metro and already a lot of work is taking root in Nelson Mandela.

Patrick:
The media is beginning to pick up on this. You’re covering so many protests one by one but its connecting the dots and seeing the pattern that is the challenge for all of us.

VO: 10
This growing disillusionment clearly took centre stage when the party convened in Midrand for the National General Council last weekend. They confronted some uncomfortable truths.

Claire link:
The ANC’s own figures reflect that they are losing support. Could the political tide be turning.

VO: 5”
ANC membership has reportedly dropped by more than 450 000.

Prof Maluleke:
A parties numbers are a very important indicator of the parties connection that is has, the resonance it has with citizens so the ANC should be concerned.

VO: 8”
The ANC is fighting this battle on several fronts - their research also reportedly yrevealed that there is a growing disconnect with the black middle class.

Prof:
They feel, and they are probably correct that the black middle class whom they created is slowly walking away from the ANC, Where would they go?

Claire:
What are the challenges with that demographic?

Zizi:
We need to review our strategies and the way we talk to our people. Ordinary people largely depend on the state for their livelihood. The black middle class they don’t depend on the state. These are the people who look at the stateand look for efficiency, they look at issues of corruption and so on,

VO: 10”
The party appears to have realized that their brand needs some serious panelbeating which is why the intregrity committee and corruption busting took centre stage this past weekend.

Zizi:
These are the issues that I think that we should deal with decisively. Because it’s a cancer. Corruption is stealing, ubusela. And these are issues that are important as a leading party.

VO:
Despite these challenges in hotspots like Kyasands where people are angry and frustrated, ma Miriam’s support for the ANC remains unwavering.

Miriam:
I don’t blame the ANC.

Zizi:
In certain areas where there has been very violent service delivery protests, come elections and the people voted for the ANC overwhelmingly in those areas.

Prof Maluleke:
It’s a little bit like a dysfunctional couple who communicate with each other in the messiest ways available. It doesn’t mean that they no longer love each other, they just hate what the other is doing. I also think people honestly believe they don’t have an alternative to the ANC.

VO: 8”
We’re likely to see an intensification of these violent service delivery strikes as we head towards the elections. Professor Bond says we’re ripe for it.

Patrick:
The world’s worst income inequality by all major measures, the world’s most most corrupt capitalist class according to Price Waterhouse Coopers and the World Economic Forum’s finding for the fourth year running the world’s most angry working class - put it all together and it’s a laboratory for some desperately needed changes.


Promo 1:

VO: 6”
We had more than 1900 violent service delivery protests last year – is this a sign of simmering dissent?

Richard Ndabase:


VO: 3
And is the political tide turning?



Promo 2

VO: 8
With service delivery protests on the rise and ANC membership numbers dwindling we ask is it time the ANC ups its game?

Prof Maluleke:
Resonance …and the ANC should be concerned.


Promo 3:

VO: 10”
We have one of the most unequal societies in the world. With service delivery protests an almost daily occurrence we ask is South Africa reaching its tipping point?
